brief.head: Gujarati v Bengali
brief.text: Families that take to eq­ui­ties com­pound wealth across gen­er­a­tions, Ajay Shah said, cit­ing US pa­pers. He called it a major fac­tor in the ris­ing gulf be­tween Gujarati and Bengali wealth. {110-C04}

brief.head: No equity, no plan
brief.text: Someone doing spread­sheet cal­cu­la­tions told Shah that with­out the eq­uity pre­mium, the num­bers can­not square for any nor­mal af­flu­ent per­son, who will be mis­er­able in old age. {110-S03}

brief.head: Her own password
brief.text: Every woman, Shah said, should know her sav­ings rate, what an index fund is, who her ser­vice provider is and the pass­word to her own ac­count. {110-C10}

brief.head: Two $500 bills
brief.text: Firms are ig­nor­ing two pools of tal­ent, Shah said: women with chil­dren who want flex­i­bil­ity, and older peo­ple who no longer want to show up at 9 a.m. {110-C11}

brief.head: Finance as hygiene
brief.text: Personal fi­nance is hy­giene, like health, Shah said: pay the one-time cost of learn­ing the ba­sics, and then about fif­teen min­utes a month is enough. {110-C09}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on money for a very long life
lead.head: Retire the question

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 110

body: A friend of Amit Varma’s asked him to put one ques­tion to Ajay Shah: how much wealth do you need to re­tire? Varma calls Shah a pic­ture of calm. Yet each time he asked, he said, “vi­o­lence re­sulted.”

After a third re­fusal, Shah gave in. In Varma’s telling, he agreed to a whole episode “be­cause it is a stupid ques­tion, but it is an im­por­tant ques­tion be­cause peo­ple have it on their minds”. {110-S01}
Shah’s an­swer was that there is no good an­swer. People who pin their sense of safety on a num­ber, and reach it, he said, “are set­ting them­selves up for grief”. What they need is a process.
## A very long life

The trou­ble starts with longevity. Hunter-gatherers lived thirty or forty years; in the age of agri­cul­ture you died by fifty or sixty. A healthy, af­flu­ent per­son today, Shah said, faces “an un­be­liev­able life span prob­lem”.
He pointed to Nomsita, a 21-year-old on the crew. Imagining her as an ac­tive lit­tle old lady paraglid­ing at 121, he said, is “not at all a rad­i­cal propo­si­tion”.
Traditional cul­ture, with chil­dren nearby to care for the old, was built for medium life­spans. It is, Shah said, ill-suited to this world.

Yet long hori­zons also give com­pound­ing more po­tency. If eq­ui­ties de­liver a real dou­bling every ten years, he said, that is 4x in twenty years, 8x in thirty, 16x in forty and 32x in fifty. That, he said, is the coun­ter­point to the longevity prob­lem. {110-C02}
## The basic cat­e­chism

The recipe is short: save a lot, buy di­ver­si­fied eq­uity index funds rather than in­di­vid­ual shares, and spread the money across the world. Shah’s rule is to take the top 20 democ­ra­cies on the Freedom House list and put about 5 per cent in each.

That roughly dou­bles the risk-adjusted re­turn com­pared with stay­ing in India alone. Diversifying all over the world, he said, is “a free lunch. Why would any­body ever be stuck in one coun­try?” {110-C03}

What the recipe will not give you is a num­ber. Shah listed three strikes against the re­tire­ment spread­sheet: you can­not know your re­turns, you can­not know the cost of what you will con­sume, and you can­not know your­self.
“There is one most im­por­tant thing which you don’t know any­thing about, which is you, which is your heart,” he said. {110-C05}
The yearn­ing for a locked-down plan, he ar­gued, comes from in­se­cu­rity. Better to do the hy­giene, ac­cept rad­i­cal un­cer­tainty and “deal with the fu­ture as it comes”.
## Nobody re­ally re­tires

Even the word re­tire­ment, Shah said, comes from an in­dus­trial age in which you stopped work at fifty-five and died by sixty. People who drop into true re­tire­ment suf­fer a rapid col­lapse in health.
If you hate your life, he said, the an­swer is to rein­vent it, not idle­ness. Change course, by all means, but stay en­gaged with work and with peo­ple.
Part of the job be­longs to the state: steady 4 per cent in­fla­tion, no fis­cal cri­sis, law and order, work­ing mar­kets, and no cap­i­tal con­trols, which Shah called im­moral.
The prize, he said, is that an or­di­nary per­son should be able to buy an index fund and for­get about it. {110-C12}
Varma closed with ad­vice of his own: in­vest in great music. The Led Zeppelin CD be­side Shah may be worth­less now, he said, “but the music re­mains with you”.

second.label: China’s missing premium
second.head: A miracle with a hole
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a fast-growing economy whose stock market never paid its people

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on China’s missing equity premium

body: China grew fast, yet it is sin­gu­lar, Ajay Shah said, in being a coun­try where eq­uity index per­for­mance never hap­pened. Perhaps the GDP data is a bit fake; per­haps the gov­ern­ment grabbed what­ever wealth was cre­ated. {#fakegdp} He thinks both have been hap­pen­ing.

Capital con­trols then trapped people’s money at home. Unable to plan for long lives, house­holds piled into prop­erty. “Everybody in China id­i­ot­i­cally buys real es­tate,” Shah said, and many houses will never be used. {#realestate}
He called it the hole in the heart of the China model: a suc­cess for the state, not for its peo­ple. His plea was to “look at it from the view­point of the peo­ple, not the state”. {110-C14}

quote.text: We cre­ate a coun­try for the ben­e­fits of the peo­ple, not for the ar­ro­gance and the pride of the state per­son­nel.

third.head: Cheap phones, dear doctors

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Baumol’s cost disease

body: Anything ma­chines can make will crash in price, Ajay Shah said. He had paid ₹20,000 for his phone; its level of ca­pa­bil­ity will as­suredly cost ₹1,000. {#phone}

Anything that needs peo­ple will keep get­ting dearer, be­cause GDP growth pushes wages up. Listing cooks and driv­ers, he caught him­self: “oops, driver­less cars. Scratch that.” Personal ser­vices, he said, “will go to in­fin­ity”. {110-C06}
The econ­o­mist William Baumol fig­ured this out, Shah said: a doctor’s con­sul­ta­tion will cost ever more steel as steel gets cheaper to make.

His point was not that old age will be dear. “I’m not here to take a stand on the idea that your life will be­come very ex­pen­sive,” he said. {#dontknow} “I am here to take a stand on the idea that we don’t know.”

p2.title: Forget the number
p2.deck: Why Ajay Shah calls the retirement number the wrong question, and what he would do instead {110-S01}

quote.text: So our tra­di­tional op­er­at­ing sys­tem is ill suited for this world.

photo.caption: Jeremy Siegel speaking at the ASSA Annual Meeting in Philadelphia in 2026

box.title: Two centuries of shares
box.text: Ajay Shah’s clos­ing rec­om­men­da­tion was Jeremy Siegel’s *Stocks for the Long Run*, which he called a grand book. It gives the basic in­tu­ition of two hun­dred years of eq­uity index in­vest­ing, and ev­ery­body, he said, should read it and in­ter­nalise the mes­sage deeply. {110-R01}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: An operating system for 121
sections.caption: why there is no good answer
body: Ajay Shah began by re­ject­ing the ques­tion. There is no good an­swer to how much wealth you need to re­tire, he said, and if you fall in love with an an­swer, be­ware of get­ting what you wish. What we need is “the wis­dom of ac­cept­ing un­cer­tainty about the world”.

The deeper prob­lem is longevity. In the hunter-gatherer age, he said, you grew up and rapidly died; in the age of agri­cul­ture you were gone by fifty or sixty. Young Nomsita, all of twenty-one, must now plan for 121. {110-J03}
## Built for shorter lives

Traditional cul­ture was de­signed for medium life­spans, with chil­dren nearby to care for par­ents in old age. Now the fam­ily is in de­cline: peo­ple have fewer chil­dren and spend less time with fam­ily. That raises the ques­tion of what it means to grow old. {110-C01}

Amit Varma added a prob­lem of mind­set. People treat life as a des­ti­na­tion, he said, where you reach a sum of money, re­tire and sail off into the sun­set. But life is a con­tin­u­ous process. His own big­gest fear is liv­ing longer, with more of it lost to de­men­tia. {#dementia}
~ The fram­ing may be faulty, Varma con­ceded, but the worry is valid: what must I do fi­nan­cially so that I don’t run into trou­ble as I go along?

quote.text: So our tra­di­tional op­er­at­ing sys­tem is ill suited for this world.

sections.label: The counterweight
sections.head: Paid to wait, not to gamble
sections.caption: the equity premium
body: The heart of good fi­nan­cial plan­ning, Ajay Shah said, is eq­uity in­vest­ment, and “the magic phrase is the eq­uity pre­mium”: the higher av­er­age re­turn earned for hold­ing di­ver­si­fied eq­ui­ties. The uni­verse does not pay you for fool­ish, un­di­ver­si­fied risk, only for the sys­tem­atic risk left after di­ver­si­fy­ing.

Long lives make it stronger. With a real dou­bling every ten years, he said, wealth grows 32 times in fifty, and over long decades the ups and downs tend to can­cel out. The eq­uity pre­mium is the coun­ter­point to the longevity prob­lem. {110-C02}
Small changes in the ex­pected re­turn get mag­ni­fied over such hori­zons, so the size of the pre­mium mat­ters. “You can’t be philo­soph­i­cal about it,” he said.
## From one coun­try to twenty

Diversification runs from one com­pany to many, from one in­dus­try to twenty and, the big­gie, from one coun­try to many. The United States has bad decades and Japan good ones; on av­er­age it can­cels out. Holding twenty coun­tries, Shah said, roughly dou­bles the risk-adjusted re­turn of any one alone. {110-C03}

~ The fewer years you have, the more it mat­ters. With sixty years, a 40 per cent draw­down in India alone can be rid­den out. With twenty or thirty, the an­swer is in­ter­na­tional di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion.

quote.text: So in a way, the coun­ter­point to the longevity prob­lem is the eq­uity pre­mium prob­lem.

sections.label: Three strikes
sections.head: Your heart isn’t in the sheet
sections.caption: the illusion of control
body: Retirement spread­sheets are ev­ery­where on YouTube. Ajay Shah’s ob­jec­tion is that they pre­tend to know three things no­body can know.

First, re­turns. Nobody should take a long-run av­er­age Nifty re­turn, “like 13% nom­i­nal in INR”, stick it in a spread­sheet and as­sume it will go on smoothly. {#nifty} The pre­mium is paid pre­cisely be­cause things can go wrong.

Second, what things will cost. Even the hosts’ episode *The World in 2050*, only 25 years out, sounded like sci­ence fic­tion, and they meant every claim, Shah said. Fifty or sev­enty-five years out, the world will be unimag­in­ably dif­fer­ent. {110-R07}

Prices will move with it. Machines will make goods ever cheaper while ser­vices that need peo­ple get dearer, a ten­sion the econ­o­mist William Baumol fig­ured out. People will keep ad­just­ing what they buy.
## The un­known self
Third, and most im­por­tant, you: your pref­er­ences, your val­ues, your heart. Humans, Shah said, are no­to­ri­ously bad at un­der­stand­ing what they value. {110-C05}
Could a twenty-year-old Amit Varma have de­scribed a good life at fifty-two? He could not, Varma said: there were too many un­known un­knowns.

~ The crav­ing for a locked-down num­ber, Shah ar­gued, comes from in­se­cu­rity. Whoever cal­cu­lates X money, gets it and sets off to travel the world will be un­happy when the world changes on them. {110-C07}

quote.text: We want cer­tainty be­cause we are weak and we are scared.

sections.label: What to do
sections.head: Idleness is not the answer
sections.caption: getting out of the word retirement
body: Asked for ac­tion­ables, Ajay Shah began with a word to drop. Retirement, he said, is an in­dus­trial-age idea: you re­tired at fifty-five and died by sixty. {#retire55}

In the hard data, peo­ple who go into true re­tire­ment suf­fer a rapid col­lapse in health; those who stay en­gaged with work and with peo­ple do bet­ter. Change course, by all means, and go live in a vil­lage in Himachal Pradesh. But keep doing stuff “with every last drop”. {110-C08}
Amit Varma had seen it: of two peo­ple re­tir­ing at the same age, the one who vol­un­teers at a dog shel­ter or gives tu­itions stays health­ier and hap­pier.
## A sim­ple drill
The fi­nan­cial process is short: a high sav­ings rate, and the index funds of the top 20 democ­ra­cies on the Freedom House Index. {110-R04}

What of peo­ple, women es­pe­cially, with no band­width? Shah said no­body needs to pick stocks, and op­er­at­ing the ac­counts is easy now. “It is like 3x harder to use Zerodha than it is to use Zepto.” {110-J05}

~ His sug­ges­tion for a higher sav­ings rate was to cut spend­ing on restau­rants and al­co­hol. Varma protested that Swiggy sur­vives in India be­cause of him. Shah pre­scribed boiled veg­eta­bles. “Very sad,” said Varma. {110-J06}

quote.text: If you hate your life, the an­swer is not idle­ness. If you hate your life, the an­swer is to rein­vent your life.

sections.label: Many countries
sections.head: A Magna Carta for savers
sections.caption: spreading money across the world
body: To fix in­tu­ition, Ajay Shah walked through the ex­pe­ri­ences of sev­eral coun­tries. In the United States and the UK, the basic recipe has worked over two or three hun­dred years, through two world wars and a cold war.
The one dark spell was cap­i­tal con­trols, which he said orig­i­nated with Hitler in 1933 and were gone from all rich coun­tries by the late sev­en­ties. {#hitler}
It is your money, he said, not the government’s to di­rect, and he called the free­dom to use it as you like a Magna Carta right. {110-J13}
## Three coun­tries, three fates

Japan’s mar­ket failed for some twenty years after its 1986 crash, but its peo­ple were free to in­vest abroad, and that saved them. China, Shah said, had nei­ther work­ing eq­ui­ties nor that free­dom: “the worst of all worlds”.

India sits in be­tween. Its con­trols, mer­ci­fully, are solv­able. “You need a lawyer, you need a bank, you need an ad­vi­sor, you’ll need to jump hoops,” Shah said, but it can be done and it should be done. {#lawyer}
He is proud, he said, of the Indian eq­uity market’s progress from about 1991 to about 2009–10, the story of the hosts’ episode and his paper *The Journey of Indian Finance*. {110-R09}
~ He then made Amit Varma prac­tise “in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion”, which Varma re­peated until it be­came “in­ten­tion­ally in­ter­na­tion­al­ist”.

quote.text: It’s a Magna Carta right that it’s your money and you should use your money as you like.

sections.label: The state’s part
sections.head: Pour concrete on four per cent
sections.caption: what citizens should demand of the state
body: What should cit­i­zens de­mand? Ajay Shah listed five things, start­ing with in­fla­tion. If you have 10 per cent in­fla­tion for four years, he said, you have knocked out 50 per cent of your port­fo­lio. {#inflation}

The is­suer of the rupee should be legally ac­count­able for 4 per cent, “not too low, not too high”, year after year. India’s in­fla­tion tar­get­ing began only on 20 February 2015, so the state must prove it­self for the next ninety years. {#feb2015}
## No cri­sis, no gang­sters
Second, no fis­cal cri­sis. India’s debt-to-GDP ratio, he said, is about twice what it ought to be, and should be halved over the next twenty-five years.

Third, law and order, be­cause vi­o­lence is equally bad whether it comes from a gang­ster or a gov­ern­ment em­ployee. Fourth, work­ing firms and fi­nan­cial mar­kets, so that an in­di­vid­ual can sim­ply buy an eq­uity index fund and for­get about it. {110-C12}
Fifth, no cap­i­tal con­trols, which Shah called im­moral, as bad as re­fus­ing some­one an im­ported dengue vac­cine. {110-C13}

~ Amit Varma had a quib­ble with Shah’s word “so­ci­etal”, and a scheme for those who dis­trust the state: a cryp­tocur­rency called ev­ery­thing coin, run on an al­go­rithm the hosts could not re­veal. {#coin}

quote.text: It’s as bad as telling you that a cer­tain vac­cine can­not be given to you be­cause it is im­ported.
So that in the end, the fruit of the labour is that an in­di­vid­ual should be able to dumbly buy an eq­uity index fund and for­get about it.

p3.title: Tales from the long run
p3.deck: Four stories from the episode, and what each says about planning a long life

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a crash, two decades, and an open door
stories.head: Twenty dead years, one way out
body: To show why own­ing one coun­try is not enough, Ajay Shah turned to Japan. Through the 1970s and 1980s, he said, there was “a giant mess in the Japanese macro econ­omy”, and it led to a great crash that began in 1986.
What sur­prised him was what fol­lowed. For a very long time after 1986, the eq­uity mar­ket sim­ply did not de­liver. There was a twenty-year pe­riod in which eq­ui­ties did badly. {#twenty}
For a saver who held on through that stretch, it was fright­en­ing. Anyone hold­ing Japan alone, Shah said, “re­ally got a ter­ri­ble and abysmal per­for­mance” from the eq­uity port­fo­lio.

But Japan was an ad­vanced democ­racy, and there were no cap­i­tal con­trols. The Japanese gov­ern­ment, he said, did not in­ter­fere with the free­dom of its peo­ple. {#japanfree} A Japanese saver could spread money all over the world.

That was the res­cue. “The way to pro­tect fi­nan­cial plan­ning through the very un­usual catas­tro­phe of the Japanese econ­omy from 1986 to 2006 to 2010 was global di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion,” Shah said. {110-S04}

Recipe one, hold­ing an eq­uity index fund at home, would not have worked in Japan for that pe­riod. Recipe two would have: go to the Freedom House list, find the top 20 democ­ra­cies of the world and buy their index funds.
~ Shah had al­ready set Japan be­side the United States and the UK, where the basic recipe worked for two or three hun­dred years. Japan is the case where recipe one failed for twenty years.
stories.why: Even a rich, free country’s mar­ket can fail its savers for decades. Owning the home index is recipe one; own­ing the in­dexes of many democ­ra­cies is recipe two, and recipe two is what sur­vives.
stories.postscript: Next came China, which Shah called “a re­ally bad sit­u­a­tion”: no eq­uity per­for­mance, and cap­i­tal con­trols be­sides. {110-R08}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Japan’s lost decades

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the future nobody could have predicted
stories.head: A million booths, then none
body: Ajay Shah asked whether a twenty-year-old Amit Varma could have de­scribed a good life at fifty-two. Varma said he could not.
At twenty, he said, he could never have imag­ined smart­phones, or AI that turns im­ages into video, or hold­ing the means of pro­duc­tion to make YouTube shows and films. {#smartphones}

His ex­am­ple was the tele­phone. “Before mo­bile tele­phony came, India had a mil­lion STD booths,” he said. “Today we have none.” Those jobs were lost, but the econ­omy and pro­duc­tiv­ity grew, and new jobs sprouted in ways no­body could have imag­ined. {110-S05}

~ The good sur­prises, he be­lieves, come through tech­nol­ogy, be­cause that is what his­tory has shown. The bad ones come from pol­i­tics and geopol­i­tics: what if there is a war, or hy­per­in­fla­tion, and sav­ings get wiped out? {#war}
stories.why: The fu­ture ar­rives as un­known un­knowns. To think it can be lin­early ex­trap­o­lated from today’s world, Varma said, is “just stupid”. Better to plan a process of liv­ing, so that you are al­ways kind of okay.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on India’s vanished STD booths

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the middle-class script he once followed
stories.head: Burning money, safely
body: Twenty years ago, Amit Varma said, Ajay Shah’s per­sonal fi­nance mod­ule might have changed his life. He doubts he would have un­der­stood it then, or even been re­cep­tive.

He had fol­lowed the typ­i­cal Indian mid­dle-class script: get an ed­u­ca­tion, have a ca­reer, put the salary in the bank, and keep it in fixed de­posits or a sav­ings ac­count to be safe. {#script}

It took him a long time to see that this was a los­ing propo­si­tion. Inflation is so high, he said, that money kept in a sav­ings ac­count, as he kept his for the long­est time, is money being burned. {110-S02}
~ The script has its fears too. The mo­ment you say stock mar­ket, Varma said, the mid­dle-class mind thinks of risk and of los­ing ev­ery­thing, “which is ab­so­lutely not the case”. {#stockmarket}
stories.why: The safe de­fault can qui­etly de­stroy wealth. What you want, Varma said, is not to rely only on being able to work for a liv­ing, but to let what­ever money you make work for you.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on money left in a savings account

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s trivia from an ageing Japan
stories.head: Minister for lonely hearts
body: Amit Varma came across a piece of trivia the day be­fore record­ing, one he felt he should have known, since he fol­lows gov­ern­ments closely: Japan has had a min­is­ter for lone­li­ness for a few years. {110-S06}

The post is mainly for old peo­ple. Japan is going through the op­po­site de­mo­graphic tran­si­tion to India’s, with tons of old peo­ple and ques­tions of lone­li­ness, so the min­is­ter or­gan­ises scrab­ble and car­rom tour­na­ments to keep them oc­cu­pied.
Varma called it a very first-world prob­lem, and said Indian prob­lems would be very dif­fer­ent.
~ It fit­ted Ajay Shah’s warn­ing that the fam­ily, the old sup­port sys­tem for the aged, is in de­cline. Japan, Shah said, is al­ready build­ing ro­bots to give frail old peo­ple a bath. {#bath}

quote.text: Japan now ap­par­ently, in fact for a few years, has a min­is­ter for lone­li­ness.

quiz.q: How many STD booths did Amit Varma say India had before mobile telephony?
quiz.a: A mil­lion, he said; today India has none, yet the econ­omy grew.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 110. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jeremy Siegel (Xuthoria, CC BY-SA 4.0).

shelf.title: Stocks for the Long Run
shelf.creator: Jeremy Siegel
shelf.why: It builds the basic in­tu­ition from two hun­dred years of eq­uity index in­vest­ing, which is the foun­da­tion of the episode’s whole ar­gu­ment.

shelf.title: Led Zeppelin
shelf.creator: Led Zeppelin
shelf.why: His ad­vice is to ‘in­vest in great music.’ The CD may now be worth­less, but the music stays with you and shapes who you be­come.

shelf.title: International Diversification Calculation spreadsheet
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It lets you play with eq­uity index per­for­mance, hold­ing pe­ri­ods, and re­ward-to-risk ra­tios, and see how much risk smarter di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion re­moves.

shelf.title: Freedom House Index
shelf.creator: Freedom House
shelf.why: Freedom House’s democ­racy rank­ings, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bot­tom: a de­cent, easy-to-use mea­sure.

shelf.title: Zerodha
shelf.why: Ajay says mod­ern firms like Zerodha, along with global firms, do an ex­cel­lent job and make op­er­at­ing these ac­counts easy.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The World in 2050 (Ep 106 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A play­ful but se­ri­ous at­tempt to imag­ine the world 25 years out, from swarms of cheap drones in war to how re­la­tion­ships might be or­gan­ised once love, sex, com­pan­ion­ship and par­ent­ing come apart.

shelf.title: The China Model is Broken (Ep 16 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Chinese state con­trol and in­dus­trial pol­icy caused deep prob­lems be­hind the cherry-picked EV and solar suc­cesses: Xi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion and na­tion­al­ism, cap­i­tal con­trols, real-estate over­build­ing, the exit of for­eign­ers and a failed eq­uity mar­ket.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

shelf.title: The journey of Indian finance
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s eco­nomic his­tory of Indian fi­nance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to mag­is­te­rial and the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Ep 48 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Ep 68 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

laughs.text: Amit in­tro­duces Ajay as a pic­ture of calm, ‘ab­so­lute shanti’, yet ask­ing him the re­tire­ment ques­tion three times pro­duced ‘violence’. Ajay’s even­tual reply: ‘I am a man of peace. Make episodes not war.’
Ajay on longevity, point­ing to the 21-year-old crew mem­ber Nomsita: she has to re­al­is­ti­cally plan to be ‘an ac­tive lit­tle old lady doing paraglid­ing at one twenty one.’
Ajay catches him­self mid-argument about ris­ing wages: ‘the price you will pay for a cook, for a driver, oops, driver­less cars. Scratch that.’

When Ajay sug­gests redi­rect­ing restau­rant and al­co­hol spend­ing into sav­ings, Amit protests: ‘Alcohol, though I don’t have, but Swiggy is sur­viv­ing in India be­cause of me. Why do you want to mess with that?’ The an­swer is to make boiled veg­eta­bles, and Amit mourns: ‘Very sad. Very sad.’
Amit’s offer to Chinese view­ers trapped by cap­i­tal con­trols: ‘You send an apart­ment my way or a full house, the coun­try villa, per­haps, and I will share the pass­word of my Zerodha ac­count.’

Baumol’s cost dis­ease: econ­o­mist William Baumol’s in­sight that labour-intensive ser­vices keep ris­ing in price rel­a­tive to goods. Ajay il­lus­trates it as the steel price of a doctor’s con­sul­ta­tion that keeps climb­ing.
Hitler, 1933: Ajay says cap­i­tal con­trols orig­i­nated with Hitler and had dis­ap­peared from all rich coun­tries by the late sev­en­ties.
Magna Carta: Ajay calls the free­dom to use your money as you like ‘a magna carta right.’
